extracted.intended_audience: writers of periodical essays, didactic fables, and moral satire (Spectator-style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short didactic pieces—letters, moral essays, fables, and humorous sketches—for a periodical audience, emphasizing methods of persuasion, types of fable, and rhetorical devices. Focuses on tonality (touches of nature), use of anecdote, classical models, and modes of satire/advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor touches of nature over wit
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am more pleased with a Letter that is filled with Touches of Nature than of Wit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, affecting detail and sincere emotion in correspondence and short essays rather than mere cleverness; examples: the sympathetic letter about a reconciled daughter is held up as superior. Anti‑pattern: a piece that is only witty but cold or artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with a remarkable illustrative story
rubrics_metrics.description: "I shall therefore conclude my Paper with a very remarkable Story..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End a moral or persuasive paper with a striking anecdote from history or chronicle to drive home the point. Use well‑chosen historical exempla (e.g., the Eginhart/Imma story) to illustrate moral lessons and move the reader emotionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete domestic details to support moral claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and complaints are illustrated by close particulars (letters hidden in a band‑box, a scroll of Latin as a settlement, best lace in the shop, precise appointments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster credibility and sympathy by supplying tangible, sensory, and documentary detail in narratives or complaints. Such specifics make accusations vivid and support calls for social or legal redress; anti‑pattern: vague abstractions without verifiable particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ quantitative and historical reasoning in political argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay on Lewis XIV estimates inhabitants gained and lost, army casualties, effects of famine and emigration to weigh conquest's true profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about statecraft or national policy, use numbers, chronological accounting, comparisons (losses vs gains), and historical analogies (e.g., Pyrrhus) to make the moral and pragmatic point concrete and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use periodical essays to advocate social change by public moral pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is in the Power of you... to make it as infamous to rob a poor Creature of her Honour as her Cloaths."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy moral outrage, public narrative, and shaming through essays to press for social or legal reform. Make proposed changes intelligible and emotionally resonant to readers so public opinion will back enforcement or new norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable type: animal/vegetable narratives for simple morals
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Fables I have here mentioned are raised altogether upon Brutes and Vegetables..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animals, plants, and non‑human figures when the moral is simple and universal; these make lessons accessible and palatable. Mix in human characters only when the moral requires human particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable type: allegorical personification of passions and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another kind of fable "in which the Actors are Passions, Virtues, Vices, and other imaginary Persons of the like Nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For philosophical or complex moral themes, personify abstractions (Pleasure, Pain, Virtue, Vice) and stage their interactions. Examples cited: Homer (interpreted allegorically), Spencer's Fairy‑Queen; this form suits elevated or sustained allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey instruction without offending the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nathan's Fable... had so good an Effect, as to convey Instruction to the Ear of a King without offending it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tone, example, and vehicle (animal fable, allegory) so the moral point reaches the intended audience without alienating or embarrassing them—particularly important when addressing superiors or sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive fables from philosophical or observed truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay imagines Socrates' reflection on pleasure and pain and then converts that observation into an allegory about Pleasure and Pain being married and sharing mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base allegories on general observations or philosophical insights; abstract phenomena (e.g., pleasure/pain cycles) make strong seeds for fables if translated into coherent personified narratives that illuminate human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine reader submissions, public adverts, and small oddities for humour
rubrics_metrics.description: A new vein of humour 'carries him much further' as correspondents send in curiosities (e.g., Nicholas Hart's seasonal sleeping) and advertisements which can be turned into papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real notices, reader letters, and eccentric facts as raw material for humorous or satirical pieces; serializing and following up a hinted theme lets a writer expand comic territory and engage readers’ contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground style and authority in classical exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent appeals to Aesop, Horace, La Fontaine, Plato, Xenophon, Boileau, Spencer and other classical/modern authorities are used to justify and illustrate the forms of fable and essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite respected classical and contemporary models to validate stylistic choices and teach by example; referring to established authorities both instructs readers and lends credibility to the argument about form and effect.
